content.p: Late on the night of 18 February 1983, three young men walked into a gambling club hidden in the basement of an old hotel in Seattle's Chinatown. By the time they left, thirteen people were dead. The victims had been tied up, robbed and shot in the head. A fourteenth, a gambling-game dealer named Wai Yok Chin, survived, and he later testified against all three men.

Two of the three, Kwan Fai "Willie" Mak and Benjamin Ng, were convicted of murder. The third, Wai Chiu "Tony" Ng, fled to Canada, was brought back, and was acquitted of the killings; a jury found him guilty of robbery and assault. The case stayed in the courts for years because of Mak's death sentence. Washington's Supreme Court called the crime one that "set a new gauge for cowardly murder in this state". It remains the deadliest mass murder in the state's history, according to KING 5.
content.h2: A room with a long history
content.p: The club stood in the Louisa Hotel, a three-storey brick building put up in 1909 at the heart of the International District, at the corner of South King Street and Maynard Alley South. According to HistoryLink.org, the basement beside the alley had held a Chinese social club since the Prohibition years, when another speakeasy operated on the far side of the same building. That social club, renamed the Wah Mee Club, became a place for some of the highest-stakes gambling in the region.

KIRO 7, publishing a HistoryLink account by Todd Matthews and Walt Crowley, described a club dating back to the early 1920s and patronised mostly by relatively wealthy restaurant owners and business people from the Chinese community. The same account says that beat officers added to their pay by tolerating illegal gambling in Chinatown, for a price. FOX 13 added that the club operated illegally. A Seattle police sergeant told The Seattle Times in 1993 that rooms of this kind were laid out like Nevada casinos but entered through alleys and heavily guarded, and that pots there reportedly reached $10,000.

HistoryLink says the club was reached through a succession of doors. Washington's Supreme Court noted that the robbery was of an establishment where Mak was known, and prosecutors told the Seattle Times he was the chief planner.

According to HistoryLink, Mak was 22 and had run up a gambling debt of several thousand dollars at another club where he worked. It says he picked the Wah Mee as the target and recruited two others: an old high-school classmate, Benjamin Ng, whose criminal record went back to his years as a juvenile, and Tony Ng, no relation, a quiet man who worked in his parents' restaurant in north Seattle. The Seattle Times reported in 1993 that Fowler, a detective on the case, recalled Tony Ng as "basically a good kid" who "probably wouldn't have been involved except that it was a last-minute thing".

KING 5, drawing on HistoryLink, gave this sequence. Mak and Tony Ng entered the club on the evening of 18 February, had dinner and chatted with the patrons. At about 12:30 a.m., Benjamin Ng came in and shouted "hands up". Everybody was made to lie on the floor. Tony Ng kept admitting more patrons, which nearly doubled the number inside. The men were tied, and the wallets, a woman's purse and the cash register were taken. Then, KING 5 reported, Mak and Benjamin Ng fired on the people on the floor and on the security guard until their ammunition was gone. Tony Ng later testified that Mak had told him to wait between the two security doors.

The accounts differ on timing: HistoryLink and the Seattle Times say the three men entered shortly before midnight, while KING 5 has Benjamin Ng arriving at about 12:30 a.m. Seattle detectives counted more than 30 shots fired at the fourteen victims. The attorney who represented the three men told KING 5 that they left with about $20,000.

The state Supreme Court, summarising the evidence in Mak's case, said that each person in the club was shot in the head as they lay bound. Twelve died on the floor. One died shortly afterwards at Harborview Hospital. The fourteenth victim survived to identify the gunmen, including Mak, whom he knew.

Chin, who was in his early sixties, according to HistoryLink, was a dealer of pai kau, a gambling game played with Chinese dominoes. KING 5 reported his testimony: that he managed to move beneath a gambling table despite being tied, that he was only wounded, and that he came to after hearing shouting and banging at the club's security doors. HistoryLink says he freed himself from the nylon cords and staggered out to look for help.

Ten years later the Seattle Times reported that he, then 71, had never spoken publicly about the killings. "Wai is pretty stoic," said Gary Fowler, the Seattle police detective who was among the first officers at the scene and was one of two assigned to keep Chin safe until the men were brought to justice. Fowler said Chin's view was that "it happened, it's over and let's move on".
Fowler himself padlocked the club's doors with a chain after investigators learned what the room could tell them. In 1993 he believed they had not been opened since.

Mak and Benjamin Ng were arrested within hours, KING 5 and HistoryLink both reported, and were charged with multiple counts of murder and robbery. Benjamin Ng received a sentence of life without any possibility of parole in August 1983. Mak, who was tried separately before a jury, was convicted of all thirteen counts of first-degree aggravated murder and one count of first-degree assault, the Washington Supreme Court recorded. The same jury, in a separate sentencing stage, found unanimously that no mitigating circumstances justified leniency, and the trial judge sentenced him to death. KING 5 dates that sentence to October 1983.

The Supreme Court reviewed the two-week trial record and nearly 1,000 pages of appeal briefs, and concluded that Mak had been fairly tried. It affirmed his conviction and death sentence. Among his fifty-two assignments of error was a claim that prosecutors had told one story at Benjamin Ng's trial, that Ng held the murder weapon and fired the fatal shots, and another at Mak's. The court said the argument rested on a "factually incorrect basis" and rejected it.

Tony Ng stayed free for nearly two years. KING 5 said he was found working in Calgary, Alberta, under the alias Jim Wong, and captured in October 1984. The King County prosecutor's office later said he had admitted to Seattle police that he took part in the robberies and was armed, and that he denied shooting anyone. He was extradited and tried on aggravated murder and robbery charges. HistoryLink says a clause in the extradition agreement meant he did not face the death penalty.

At trial, he told jurors he took part only because Mak had threatened to kill him and his family. The jury was instructed on duress. The prosecutor's office said afterwards that duress is not a defence to murder, but that because prosecutors did not object to the instruction, it became the law of the case. The jury convicted Tony Ng of thirteen robbery counts (first degree) and one assault count (second degree), and acquitted him of murder. He was sentenced in April 1985 to 30 years to life. HistoryLink says his appeal, which argued that jurors who accepted duress as to the murders should have accepted it on the other charges, was unsuccessful.

Mak's sentence became the part of the case that would not close. Before a federal hearing, The Seattle Times reported that Mak, then 30, had already spent seven years fighting to save his life. At the time, his lawyers were asking Judge William Dwyer, a federal judge in Seattle, to find that Mak's trial lawyers had been ineffective, because they failed to present humanising evidence at the penalty phase. The paper noted that Mak's lawyers argued his trial lawyers never called his parents to testify, whereas at Benjamin Ng's trial his mother had bowed to jurors and begged for mercy. The state's lawyers countered that Mak could not meet the legal test for ineffective assistance. The paper also listed facts the state's lawyers planned to raise, which it said Mak had admitted to the jury, including that he, Benjamin Ng and Tony Ng had planned other robberies involving tying up and killing victims, and that he had watched Benjamin Ng shoot a passing jogger while the two dumped a stolen safe in Lake Washington.

By February 1993, the Seattle Times reported that a US District Court had overturned Mak's death sentence and that the state had gone to the US Supreme Court in December to appeal. An assistant state attorney general told the paper no hearing date had been set, and the deputy prosecutor who had tried the case, Robert Lasnik, by then a Superior Court judge, said a new sentencing trial would force the public to "relive that whole awful case again". He called it "twenty years and no ending".

The sources do not agree on which court ended the death sentence. KING 5 says the Washington Supreme Court overturned it in 1991, while the Seattle Times in 1993 attributed the 1991 ruling to U.S. District Judge William Dwyer, on the ground that Mak's trial lawyers had failed to present evidence that might have spared his life. Every source that states the end result agrees: Mak was resentenced to life without parole and is serving it. In 2013 the Seattle Times described both Mak and Benjamin Ng as serving life sentences without the possibility of parole.

Tony Ng was rejected for parole five times, according to The Seattle Times. In 2013 the state's Indeterminate Sentence Review Board voted three to one to grant it. His sentence fell under Washington's old indeterminate sentencing rules, under which the board decides how much of a sentence is served. The King County prosecutor's office said the board had gradually accelerated his service on individual counts until one robbery count remained.

The board's chair, Lynne DeLano, said the decision had taken a long time. She said Ng "consistently denied he was involved in the shooting" and that his remorse seemed real. In a 2009 interview with Northwest Asian Weekly, quoted by the Times, he said: "I always ask myself why. Why wasn't I strong enough to say no?" He was described as a model prisoner who taught drafting to other inmates and folded origami animals that were sold to fund a youth programme.

The county's prosecutor, Dan Satterberg, opposed release. He said that had Ng been convicted under current law, firearm enhancements alone would have carried a 70-year term with no time off for good behaviour. "There is little doubt that Tony Ng caught some breaks in his favor that he did not deserve," Satterberg said, "but the verdict of the jury set in motion the possibility of his eventual release." Doris Wong Estridge, a distant relative of one of the victims, Wing Wong, had long pressed for him to stay in prison. Board staff said people who contacted them to oppose his release included "survivors".

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents flew Ng, then 58, from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on a Tuesday in May 2014, and he arrived in Hong Kong the next day, spokesman Andrew Munoz said. He had served 28 years by the Seattle Times count; KING 5 said 30.

KING 5 named twelve of the victims: John Loui, Moo Min Mar, Jean Mar, Henning Chin, Lung Wing Chin, Hung Fat Gee, Chinn Lee Law, Dewey Mar, George Mar, Jack Mar, Wing Wong and Gim Lun Wong. The Seattle Times said the dead were twelve men and one woman of Chinese-American background. Ron Chew, an editor at the International Examiner, told KING 5 that the neighbourhood regarded many of them as uncles, and that the killings were "gut-wrenching" for a community where people knew the families.

In 1993, Assunta Ng, publisher of the Seattle Chinese Post, said people in the neighbourhood did not want to remember it: they wanted "happy things, positive things that can help our young people". Yet Fowler and others told the same reporter that the massacre was a turning point. Community leaders, he said, came forward to help the police in ways they never had, finding witnesses and translators. City councilwoman Cheryl Chow recalled that her mother, then a county councilwoman, was called in to help identify victims, and asked why the city had not had translators or better human services in place. Afterwards, she said, the community focused on giving Asian youths alternatives to gangs.

The Wah Mee was never reopened. A fire of unknown origin tore through the Louisa Hotel on Christmas Eve 2013. HistoryLink reports that a partial demolition in April 2015 removed the section including the former club, and that a groundbreaking for the redevelopment, with 84 new apartments planned, was held in February 2018. KING 5 says affordable rental housing now stands where the club was. Chew said the coverage of the massacre, even in recent years, had fed stereotypes about the neighbourhood.
